outcome: Since 26 January 2024 no source I could read has added, bounded or disputed any idoneal number: the list stands at Euler and Gauss's 65 (largest 1848), conjectured complete. The only in-window items that could bear on the count are unrefereed Riemann-hypothesis and Landau-Siegel preprints (Weicun Zhang, from 22 October 2025), which I could not read in full, and a finite computational zero-free check (Lu, Zaman, Zhao, February 2026) that does not bear on the count.
problem_asks: (1) Whether there are exactly 65 idoneal numbers, i.e. whether any positive integer beyond Euler's list (largest 1848) is idoneal. (2) The three options 65, 66 or 67 correspond to zero, one or two further idoneal numbers, so the question is how many extra ones exist, if any. (3) The idoneal notion is Euler's: a positive integer D such that every integer with exactly one representation x^2 +/- D y^2 (x^2 coprime to D y^2) is a prime power or twice one; equivalently, n is idoneal iff it is not expressible as ab + bc + ca with distinct positive integers a, b, c. The statement does not restrict to square-free or fundamental cases, so non-square-free idoneal numbers (4, 9, 12, 16, 18, 25 and the rest) count toward the total. (4) The statement asks for the count, not for a proof of completeness by any particular method and not for a size bound on a hypothetical extra term; resolving 65 versus 66 or 67 settles it either way.

events.what_happened: S. Chowla proved that the set of idoneal numbers is finite (paper 'An extension of Heilbronn's class-number theorem', Quarterly Journal of Mathematics 5 (1934) 304-307, as cited by OEIS A000926). The result gives finiteness only, with no explicit bound on the largest idoneal number. Read: OEIS A000926 comments and MathPages 'Numeri Idonei', which states that Chowla proved in 1934 that the number of numeri idonei is finite. The 1934 paper itself was not read.
events.delivers: Finiteness of the set of idoneal numbers. No explicit bound and no count.
events.remains: Whether the set is exactly the 65 known numbers or contains one or two more; an explicit bound on any further idoneal number.

checked_by.who: Quarterly Journal of Mathematics (Oxford), journal of record for the 1934 paper
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (inferred from the OEIS citation; the article itself was not read)

events.direction: Finiteness only, consistent with the 65 list being complete. Does not decide between 65 and 66 or 67.

events.what_happened: Euler, 'Illustratio paradoxi circa progressionem numerorum idoneorum sive congruorum', Nova Acta Academiae Scientarum Imperialis Petropolitinae 15 (1806) 29-32 (E725). The arXiv English translation (math/0507352, first posted July 2005) has the abstract: 'In this paper Euler shows that there are no additional square idoneal numbers aside from 1, 4, 9, 16, and 25.' The sources do not say when Euler first wrote the argument, so the 1806 publication year may be later than the first written argument.
events.revisions: English translation on arXiv, math/0507352, first version 2005-07-18 (translation, not a new argument).
events.delivers: Restricted case: the square idoneal numbers are exactly 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25, all of which are on the list of 65.
events.remains: All non-square idoneal numbers, including the 60 on the list that are not squares, and any unknown idoneal number of any kind.
events.doubts: The sources do not state when Euler first wrote the argument, and I did not read the Latin or the translation's proof.
events.direction: Consistent with the list of 65. Settles only the squares, a restricted case.

events.what_happened: Grube (1874) is credited, in secondary summaries I could not open, with proving that Euler's definition of idoneal numbers is equivalent to one class per genus for discriminants -4n. Kani's 2011 survey, as summarised in search results and not read by me, attributes to a Grube classification that an idoneal n congruent to 3 mod 4 must be 3, 7 or 15, and that an idoneal n above 288 is not congruent to 3 mod 4. This event is recorded from secondary summaries only.
events.delivers: Restricted cases, per the secondary summary: idoneal numbers congruent to 3 mod 4 are only 3, 7 and 15; idoneal numbers above 288 are not congruent to 3 mod 4. Also the equivalence of Euler's definition with one class per genus for discriminants -4n.
events.remains: Idoneal numbers congruent to 1 or 2 mod 4 above 288, and therefore whether any idoneal number exists beyond 1848.

checked_by.qualification: Arithmetic geometer; author of the 2011 survey that restates these results
checked_by.what_they_did: Restates the Grube classification (known only from a search summary of the survey; not read by me)

events.directly_checkable: Congruence restrictions can be checked by hand against the 65 listed numbers.
events.doubts: Recorded only from secondary summaries; the original 1874 paper and Kani's text were not read.
events.direction: Restricted cases consistent with the list of 65.

events.what_happened: P. J. Weinberger, 'Exponents of the class groups of complex quadratic fields', Acta Arithmetica 22 (1973) 117-124 (DOI 10.4064/aa-22-2-117-124). Wikipedia (fetched; citing Kani 2011) says results of Weinberger from 1973 imply at most two other idoneal numbers exist, and that the list is complete if GRH holds; it also says some sources wrongly claim 'at most one'. MathPages (fetched) says it is known that there can be at most one more square-free idoneal number. MathWorld (fetched) says that if any other idoneal numbers exist, there can be only one more. A search summary of the Watkins correspondence note (not readable to me) and search snippets of a Schoof/Stopple abstract say that unconditionally there is at most one more fundamental discriminant with one class per genus. I could not read the 1973 paper (the ICM copy returned 403), so its wording is unverified.
events.delivers: Conditional on GRH for L(s, chi): the 65 known idoneal numbers are the only ones. Unconditional: at most two further idoneal numbers (Wikipedia's reading, citing Kani Corollary 23), or at most one further square-free or fundamental discriminant (MathPages, MathWorld and the Schoof/Stopple snippet). The sources disagree and I could not check the 1973 text.
events.remains: Unconditionally, whether a 66th idoneal number exists and, if so, whether a 67th does; the one-or-two bound leaves 65, 66 or 67 open. Under GRH nothing remains: the list stands at 65.

checked_by.who: Acta Arithmetica (journal of record for the 1973 paper)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper; referees not identified

events.doubts: The 'one' and 'two' readings of the unconditional bound conflict across the secondary sources I read. The 1973 paper itself was not read.
events.direction: Conditionally toward completeness at 65 (GRH). Unconditionally it caps the number of extra idoneal numbers at one or two, so the question is not settled.

events.what_happened: Ernst Kani, 'Idoneal Numbers and some Generalizations', Annales des Sciences Mathematiques du Quebec 35 (2011) no. 2, 197-227. An expository survey on idoneal numbers. Wikipedia and the OEIS entry cite it for Weinberger's bound (Corollary 23, Remark 24). A ResearchGate excerpt (search summary only, not read by me) says Kani shows unconditionally that the set of idoneal numbers contains at most two integers outside Euler's list. The PDF was not readable to me (binary, and the Queen's and labmath copies failed), so this is unverified. The survey is an exposition, not a new result; it also covers a generalisation, the convenient numbers.
events.revisions: A web copy hosted by Queen's carries a PDF creation date of 2018 (metadata of a copy I could not open); version differences unknown.
events.delivers: Restates Weinberger's bounds: conditional on GRH the list is complete; unconditionally at most two further idoneal numbers (Corollary 23, per Wikipedia and the ResearchGate summary).
events.remains: Same as the Weinberger 1973 event: whether a 66th or 67th idoneal number exists.

checked_by.who: Annales des Sciences Mathematiques du Quebec, journal of record

events.doubts: The Corollary 23 statement is known to me only through Wikipedia and a search summary; the survey text was not read.
events.direction: Same as Weinberger 1973: conditional completeness at 65; unconditional bound of one or two further idoneal numbers, so 66 and 67 remain open.

events.what_happened: Kimberly Hopkins (listed under the earlier name Kimberly Spears), 'Bounds on discriminants with one class per genus', arXiv math/0401334, submitted 23 January 2004 (v2 21 July 2009). Under an assumed condition on zeros of Dirichlet L-functions, which the arXiv abstract describes as related to GUE statistics (not explicitly GRH), the paper shows that there are no discriminants with one class per genus above d_66 of about 1.9 x 10^130. A search summary says it was submitted to Acta Arithmetica; I did not confirm publication. Body not read.
events.revisions: v2 21 July 2009 (current version per arXiv page).
events.delivers: Conditional on the assumed zero-spacing hypothesis (not GRH as the abstract reads): no one-class-per-genus discriminant above d_66, about 1.9 x 10^130. Nothing unconditional.
events.remains: Unconditionally, all of the count. Under the hypothesis, the range up to about 1.9 x 10^130, which only computation or other methods could decide.
events.doubts: Conditional on a hypothesis whose exact form I did not read; the abstract says it is related to GUE statistics rather than GRH; publication status not established. The index in d_66 is as the abstract gives it, and I did not check what index 66 refers to.
events.direction: Conditional exclusion of very large discriminants, consistent with the list of 65 being complete. Says nothing about 66 or 67 below its bound.

events.what_happened: Jeff Stopple, 'Zeros of L-functions and Euler's idoneal numbers' (title from a search result; the paper's journal and date were not established). A copy of its abstract on Schoof's site, read only as a search snippet because the site redirected and then returned 404 to me, says that by generalising a technique of Montgomery and Weinberger there is no one-class-per-genus negative discriminant -d in the range 10^100 < d < 10^28000 (exponents inferred from garbled text). A UCLA spring 2004 talk abstract, 'Deuring-Heilbronn phenomenon and Euler's idoneal numbers' (search snippet; PDF unreadable to me), gives 10^61 < d < 10^25000. Neither abstract's conditionality is stated in what I could read.
events.revisions: Talk abstract (2004) gives 10^61 to 10^25000; the paper's abstract gives 10^100 to 10^28000. Read as an improvement, not confirmed.
events.delivers: Restricted range: no further one-class-per-genus negative discriminant -d with 10^100 < d < 10^28000, per the paper abstract. Nothing for d up to 10^100 or from 10^28000 upward. The sources do not establish whether this is unconditional.
events.remains: Every d outside the range. In particular the interval between the other computational results (about 3.1 x 10^20 for fundamental discriminants, see the Elsenhans-Klueners-Nicolae event) and 10^100 is not covered by any unconditional result I read; whether Stopple's method reaches it is unresolved.
events.doubts: The abstract was read through a snippet with garbled exponents, and the two quoted ranges disagree. The paper's full text was not read, and I could not establish conditionality.
events.direction: Excludes a large range of further one-class-per-genus discriminants, consistent with the list of 65 being complete. Does not reach the 66 or 67 cases below the range.

events.what_happened: Andreas-Stephan Elsenhans, Jurgen Kluners and Florin Nicolae, 'Imaginary quadratic number fields with class groups of small exponent', arXiv:1803.02056 (submitted 6 March 2018). The abstract (fetched): for negative fundamental discriminants D with class-group exponent E(D) dividing 8, the classification is given assuming no Siegel zeros exist; the paper also computes all such D with |D| <= 3.1 x 10^20 and E(D) <= 8. Published in Acta Arithmetica 193 (2020) 217-233 per an IMPAN listing (search snippet). Exponent 2 is exactly the one-class-per-genus case, so these results cover the fundamental discriminants relevant to idoneal numbers. The OEIS A000926 comment (David Radcliffe, correction dated 22 August 2026 per the OEIS page) says that the next idoneal term, if it exists, is greater than 7.75 x 10^19 by these results. That figure is smaller than the abstract's 3.1 x 10^20 and its origin is not established.
events.delivers: For negative fundamental discriminants with E(D) dividing 8: a classification assuming no Siegel zeros, and (per the abstract as written) no further such D with |D| up to 3.1 x 10^20 beyond the computed list. Since exponent 2 is the one-class-per-genus case, this bears on fundamental discriminants of idoneal type. It does not directly cover non-fundamental idoneal discriminants, such as those from n = 4, 9, 12, 16 or 18.
events.remains: Non-fundamental idoneal discriminants; any further fundamental case above 3.1 x 10^20 (or above the 7.75 x 10^19 figure the OEIS comment quotes); and the Siegel-zero dependence of the classification.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 2020 (per IMPAN listing snippet; referees not identified)

events.doubts: The abstract's 3.1 x 10^20 computation range and the OEIS comment's 7.75 x 10^19 bound disagree, and I could not resolve why. The arXiv PDF was unreadable to me, so I could not check the theorem statements, whether the exponent-2 case is covered as I infer, or whether the computation is conditional. The no-Siegel-zero hypothesis is an assumption, not a proof.
events.direction: Toward completeness for fundamental discriminants: conditional classification, plus a computed range to 3.1 x 10^20. Leaves the non-fundamental case and the large range open.

events.what_happened: John Armitage, 'Bounds on the largest prime factor of a negative discriminant with one class per genus', arXiv:2011.09401 (submitted 18 November 2020). The abstract (fetched) concerns a negative discriminant with at least 32 genera, the case that would contradict Gauss's conjecture if it had one class per genus, and argues that such a discriminant cannot have a particularly large prime factor. The method is described as similar to Baker's solution of Gauss's class number one problem. It does not mention idoneal numbers or bound their count. A search summary of the introduction (not read by me) attributes a lower bound of 9.8 x 10^18 to earlier computations, not to this paper.
events.delivers: Restricted to discriminants with at least 32 genera: a bound on their largest prime factor. Different quantity from the count of one-class-per-genus discriminants.
events.direction: Neither toward nor against 65, 66 or 67: a different question about discriminants with at least 32 genera.

events.what_happened: Yitang Zhang, 'Discrete mean estimates and the Landau-Siegel zero', arXiv:2211.02515 (submitted 4 November 2022, one version). The abstract (fetched) claims an effective lower bound L(1, chi) >> (log D)^(-2022) for real primitive characters chi mod D, with an absolute, effectively computable constant. Scientific American (search snippet) says it has not been peer-reviewed. A 2023 commentary by Zeraoulia Rafik (arXiv:2304.12862, 7 April 2023) uses chaotic dynamics and says the analysis 'roughly proves the validity' of Zhang's results; I read its abstract, which contains no number theory and does not mention idoneal numbers or one-class-per-genus discriminants. A search summary had attributed to the commentary the statement that the claim would reduce the one-class-per-genus classification to a finite computation; I could not confirm that from the abstract. No withdrawal notice seen.
events.revisions: v1 only (per arXiv page); no later version or withdrawal seen.
events.delivers: As the abstract reads, an effective lower bound for L(1, chi) of order (log D)^(-2022). It does not list or bound idoneal numbers. A possible route to the count runs through Siegel zeros, which such a bound would exclude; that is my inference, not something a source states, and it is not verified.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, as far as this event goes; it establishes no bound on the count.
events.doubts: Not peer-reviewed (Scientific American via snippet). Zhang's 2007 preprint on the same conjecture was never published and had gaps, per a search snippet. A Manifold prediction market on the claim resolved at 5% in early 2023 (snippet). Public informal discussion exists (a Woit blog post and MathOverflow, cited in the snippets, not read by me); no published verification or refutation found. These are signals only.
events.direction: If correct, would exclude Siegel zeros (my inference). Says nothing directly about idoneal numbers.

events.what_happened: Simon Brandhorst, Serkan Sonel and Davide Cesare Veniani, 'Idoneal genera and K3 surfaces covering an Enriques surface', arXiv:2003.08914 (first version 19 March 2020 under an earlier title per search snippet; latest v7 14 April 2025; accepted in Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra, DOI 10.1016/j.jpaa.2025.107974, per the arXiv comments). The abstract (fetched) says idoneal genera are a generalisation of Euler's idoneal numbers; the authors enumerate all idoneal genera via the Smith-Minkowski-Siegel mass formula and use this to classify transcendental lattices of K3 surfaces covering an Enriques surface. The abstract gives no count; a 557 figure appears only in a search snippet of an interview.
events.revisions: v2 10 May 2020; v3 24 May 2020; v4 1 Sep 2020; v5 22 Feb 2021; v6 7 Jan 2022; v7 14 Apr 2025; accepted in JPAA (2025).
events.delivers: Enumerates idoneal genera, lattice genera that generalise Euler's idoneal numbers. Does not state a count of classical idoneal numbers and does not bear on whether 66 or 67 exist.

checked_by.who: Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra, journal of record

events.direction: A different question: a generalisation of idoneal numbers to lattice genera. No bearing on the count of classical idoneal numbers.

events.what_happened: Rick F. Lu, Asif Zaman and Haonan Zhao, 'Numerical Computations Concerning Landau-Siegel Zeros', arXiv:2602.03626 (submitted 3 February 2026). The abstract (fetched) reports a computational check that quadratic Dirichlet L-functions L(s, chi) with modulus q <= 10^10 have no real zeros for sigma >= 1 - 1/(5 log q). This is a finite check over moduli, not a proof for all q. The abstract does not mention idoneal numbers or class groups.
events.delivers: A finite numerical zero-free region for quadratic Dirichlet L-functions with modulus up to 10^10. No proof that Siegel zeros are absent for all moduli, and no bound on idoneal numbers.
events.direction: No direction on the count. Neighbouring computational work on the zero-free question that the Siegel-zero route would need.

events.what_happened: Weicun Zhang (University of Science and Technology Beijing, per search snippet), 'A Unified Proof of the Extended, Generalized, and Grand Riemann Hypothesis' (later retitled, per search snippet, with 'Based on the General Properties of L-Functions'), Preprints.org manuscript 202506.0481. Per search summaries of its version history, versions run from 22 October 2025 to 1 April 2026, labelled 'not peer-reviewed version'. It claims to prove the Extended, Generalized and Grand Riemann Hypotheses in one framework and, in later versions, that Landau-Siegel zeros are excluded. The Preprints.org page returned 403 to me, so this event rests on search-result summaries and not on the text.
events.revisions: Many versions per search summaries; framing changed between versions (earlier: Hadamard-product argument; later: entire functions as absolutely convergent products). Landau-Siegel exclusion appears only in later versions, so the scope grew.
events.delivers: Claimed, unrefereed: a proof of GRH for Dirichlet L-functions (and ERH and Grand RH). If accepted, Weinberger's 1973 GRH-conditional theorem (as cited by Wikipedia, Hopkins and Kani) would make the list of 65 complete, i.e. exclude a 66th or 67th idoneal number. The claimed Landau-Siegel exclusion would bear on the Siegel-zero hypothesis of the Elsenhans-Klueners-Nicolae classification (my inference, not checked). The claim is not established by any source I could read.
events.remains: Nothing is established by this preprint as far as I can tell. If it were accepted, GRH would close the count at 65 (inference).
events.doubts: Unrefereed. The same author has a series of Riemann-hypothesis preprints on Preprints.org (manuscript 202108.0146, many versions, per search snippets) with no acceptance that I could find, so this is a serial claim history. No expert critique, journal acceptance or identified error found in my searches. Scope grew between versions (Landau-Siegel exclusion added later). The claimed result is one of the best-known open problems, so an error or acceptance would each be decisive; none has been reported.
events.direction: If correct, toward completeness at 65 via the GRH route (inference from Weinberger's theorem). In the snippets I saw, no mention of idoneal numbers.

disputes.summary: Weinberger's unconditional bound. 'At most two' further idoneal numbers: Wikipedia (fetched, citing Kani 2011 Corollary 23), a ResearchGate excerpt of Kani (search summary only), and a convenient-numbers talk snippet. 'At most one': MathPages (fetched; square-free), MathWorld (fetched), a Schoof/Stopple abstract snippet and a Watkins correspondence summary (both fundamental discriminants). My reading, not verified against Weinberger's or Kani's text: the 'one' bound is for square-free or fundamental cases and the 'two' bound covers all idoneal numbers. Wikipedia itself says some sources wrongly claim 'one'.

Computational bounds on a further idoneal term are not reconciled: 'greater than 10^8' (McCranie 2005, OEIS); 'greater than 7.75 x 10^19' (Radcliffe, OEIS, citing Elsenhans-Klueners-Nicolae); 'at least 9.8 x 10^18' (earlier computations, per a search summary of Armitage); '|D| up to 3.1 x 10^20 computed for exponent dividing 8' (Elsenhans-Klueners-Nicolae abstract, fundamental discriminants). The OEIS page is the one quoting the lower figure.

Ranges of unconditional exclusion of one-class-per-genus discriminants: 10^100 < d < 10^28000 (Schoof-site abstract snippet, paper) versus 10^61 < d < 10^25000 (UCLA spring 2004 talk snippet). Read as earlier and later results, not confirmed.
Rosetta Code states 'at most two more' and 'no others below 1,000,000'. It is unsourced and I do not rely on it.

summary: The count is unchanged in every source I could read. The list stands at Euler and Gauss's 65 idoneal numbers, largest 1848, conjectured complete. Wikipedia (fetched; last edited 3 April 2025 per the page), OEIS A000926 (fetched; last modified 11 October 2026) and MathWorld (fetched; last updated 2 October 2026) all still pose the question as open. The main bound is Weinberger's 1973 theorem: conditional on GRH it gives completeness; unconditionally it caps the number of further idoneal numbers, which is what makes 65, 66 or 67 the question. The cap is disputed. Wikipedia and the Kani-based summaries say 'at most two'; MathPages, MathWorld and the Schoof/Stopple and Watkins snippets say 'at most one' for square-free or fundamental cases. I could not open Weinberger's paper or Kani's survey, so I cannot settle which is the theorem's own statement. Pre-2024 work narrows the search. Euler (publication 1806) settled the squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 only. Chowla (1934) proved finiteness. Hopkins (arXiv 2004) gives a conditional exclusion beyond about 1.9 x 10^130. Stopple (2004) gives an unconditional exclusion for 10^100 < d < 10^28000, read from a garbled snippet. Elsenhans, Kluners and Nicolae (arXiv 2018, Acta Arithmetica 2020) classify fundamental discriminants with exponent dividing 8 assuming no Siegel zeros, and compute to 3.1 x 10^20, which is the strongest unconditional coverage I read; it covers fundamental discriminants only, and the OEIS comment quotes a weaker 7.75 x 10^19 figure. I found no unconditional coverage in the sources I read for the gap between 3.1 x 10^20 and 10^100. In the window (since 26 January 2024) I found no new idoneal number, no claimed 66th, no improved bound and no AI-attributed result. The arXiv full-text search for 'idoneal' returns ten hits, none a new classical result in the window; the only in-window generalisation (Brandhorst, Sonel and Veniani, 'idoneal genera', JPAA 2025) is a different question. The in-window items that could bear on the count are two Landau-Siegel and Riemann-hypothesis claims. Weicun Zhang's Preprints.org series (from 22 October 2025, claiming GRH and later Landau-Siegel exclusion) would, if correct, close the count at 65 by Weinberger's GRH theorem; it is unrefereed, I could not read its text (403), and I found no expert engagement. Lu, Zaman and Zhao (February 2026) give a finite numerical zero-free check that does not bear on the count. Yitang Zhang's 2022 Landau-Siegel claim is pre-window and unrefereed; through the Siegel-zero route it could matter to the fundamental-discriminant part, but that inference is mine. On the 65/66/67 wording: a search summary of a TCNJ talk on convenient numbers (not opened; 403) says that a single extra odd n gives exactly 66 numbers and an even n comes with 4n, giving 67; this is probably the source of the three-way phrasing, but I did not verify it. AI: no source I read names any AI system in connection with idoneal numbers. Targeted AI searches (queries 5, 12, 23, 24, 32 and 37) and the Lean and Mathlib search (query 29) found nothing. The AI-math results they surfaced (OpenAI's Erdos unit-distance work, Axiom, FrontierMath) do not mention idoneal numbers. I record none_found as true on that basis, with the caveat that the search was web-only and that the Weicun Zhang preprint text was not readable to me.
competing_reading: The two-bound reading (Wikipedia, Kani Corollary 23) leaves 66 and 67 both open, which is exactly the question as posed; the one-bound reading is the same question with a tighter cap. On the other side, if either Weicun Zhang's GRH preprint or Yitang Zhang's 2022 effective bound were accepted, the GRH route (Weinberger) or the Siegel-zero route (Elsenhans-Klueners-Nicolae) would close the fundamental-discriminant count at 65 without any new search for idoneal numbers. A reader who weighs those claims as credible would call the problem settled at 65 in the window; nothing I read establishes that. A reader who weighs the claims as not credible would call the problem open with nothing in the window bearing on it.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The text of Weinberger 1973 (Acta Arithmetica 22, 117-124) and Kani 2011 Corollary 23 and Remark 24, to fix whether the unconditional cap is one or two and whether it is for fundamental discriminants or all idoneal numbers. (2) The full text of Elsenhans, Kluners and Nicolae: whether the exponent-2 case is covered as I infer, whether the 3.1 x 10^20 computation is conditional, what it says about non-fundamental discriminants, and why the OEIS figure is 7.75 x 10^19. (3) Expert review or refutation of the Weicun Zhang preprint (latest version 1 April 2026) and of Yitang Zhang's arXiv 2211.02515, including whether a v2 or withdrawal exists. (4) Stopple's paper, for conditionality and whether any result covers 3.1 x 10^20 to 10^100. (5) Any published 66th or 67th idoneal number; none found.

judgement.why: Nothing after 26 January 2024 touches the count: Lu-Zaman-Zhao is a finite zero-free check not about idoneal numbers (none), and Weicun Zhang's GRH claim never mentions idoneal numbers, bears only via a conditional reduction (none), and carries several F10 signals together (not_credible). Pre-snapshot: Weinberger's at-most-one-or-two cap and Chowla's finiteness are bounds; Euler's squares and Grube's congruence results settle restricted cases; Kani is a survey; Hopkins and the EKN classification are conditional (variant), and EKN's computation to 3.1e20 is a finite search (instances); Armitage and idoneal genera are different questions. No pre-snapshot event answers the whole question, so nothing is resolved before the snapshot either.
judgement.doubts: Whether Stopple's range exclusion is unconditional, and whether Chowla's qualitative finiteness should count as a bound, are close calls; neither changes the outcome. Weinberger's cap (one vs two) is disputed in the record's sources.
